articleTitle: Electronic arms and legs: Meeting the bionic challenge: Though still far from creating a six-million-dollar man, the progress of electronic prosthesis technology is nothing short of a biotechnical wonder
abstract: A few months ago we viewed with great pride our country's emissaries to the 23rd Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles, Calif. Watching these amazing, young athletes in action, one could not help but be reminded of the original Olympians whose bodies were to be perfect, unblemished examples of the optimum physical condition that our bodies can reach. These godlike heroes perfectly harmonized nerve and muscle into the intricate melodies of motion that gained them victory.

articleTitle: The computer revolution in medical imaging systems: Computers have become an essential part of medical imaging, where their many uses include control of hardware and image enhancement and generation
abstract: During the past eight years computers have revolutionized medical imaging technology, playing a major role in the control of electronic hardware and in the enhancement and generation of images of the interior of a patient's body. Today microcomputers, minicomputers, or both can be found in a variety of medical imaging systems, including X-ray radiography, fluoroscopy, and tomography, and nuclear medicine and magnetic resonance systems. The specific manner in which a computer carries out its functions in any of these systems varies depending on the type of system and the manufacturer. However, a generic examination of these functions as they apply to the first three systems mentioned will provide a good idea of the overall application of computers in medical imaging.

articleTitle: Instrumentation for analyzing biological cells: Research efforts are focused on the complementary use of instruments that measure and sort potential cancer cells and those that yield photometric data
abstract: Instrumentation for analyzing biological cells is a growing field that provides exciting opportunities for the engineer to make a valuable contribution to medicine and biology. At the computer cell analysis laboratory at the Cancer Research Center (CRC) in Columbia, Mo., for example, we have been interested in bridging the gap between two basic types of cell analysis instruments. The first, a flow cytometry device, is characterized by the ability to perform a small number of measurements on a large number of cells. The second, a cell image analyzer, performs analyses on images obtained from a computerized microscope and is characterized by its ability to obtain a large number of measurements on a small number of cells.

articleTitle: Looking back [Man of High Fidelity: Edwin Howard Armstrong]
abstract: Recounts the circumstances surrounding the development of FM radio and and patent and legal issues that eventually led to the suicide of its inventor Edwin Howard Armstrong. "Major" Armstrong, as he became known to friends after his commission in World War I, had spent most of his career defending his legal credentials as a great inventor in an area in which he had received about 50 patents and had conceived the regenerative feedback circuit, the superhetrodyne receiver, the superregenerative receiver, and FM broadcasting. His peers had recognized his accomplishments with awards several times, but his legal battles had reached a breaking point. Five years before his suicide, he had filed suits against RCA and NBC for infringement on his FM patents. After Armstrong's tragic death, his wife, Marion, took up his cause. Ultimately, all 21 suits of infringement on his FM patents by RCA and NBC were decided in his favor.

articleTitle: On becoming an engineer part I: The impulse function: The first of three articles examines the transition from the classroom to your first job. How should you approach it? Hit it hard with all you have
abstract: This series of three articles is not about technical engineering as you have been learning it in school. It is about your transition from the classroom to the “real world.” This article deals with your first years on the job; subsequent articles will deal with what you need to do to stay an engineer, and what your obligations to society are.

articleTitle: Job prospects '84: Optimistic, but not dramatic: Employers are optimistic about the class of '84, but caution that you should expect fewer offers and slight salary increases — And be willing to relocate
abstract: As you well know, “economic uncertainty” has been a key phrase for quite some time, and 1983 graduates certainly felt the impact of those words. Although interest rates were coming down, economic uncertainty during the 1982–83 academic year kept employers' hiring to a minimum, and caution — not expansion — was the rule of the day.

articleTitle: The EE and health care policy: A call to action: Lack of engineering involvement has led to government policies that have cast the profession in a poor light. The time is ripe for concerted action
abstract: There was a time when engineers could be proud of their technical ingenuity and not be concerned about defending their inventions. Wrapped in their research, they could feel immune to political effects. That time is no more. Today, every move the engineer makes has social, historical, ethical, and political ramifications. This impact is being particularly felt in the area of health care where engineers are blamed as much as they are praised for the consequences of the technology they have created. The time has come for reaction from the engineering community — not defensive reaction, but concerted, decisive action.

articleTitle: Unification through registration: Unification of the profession through registration will help clear the confusion about what constitutes the practice of engineering
abstract: We as engineers are at a crossroad. Our profession is in decline. There is much talk that our inventions cause strife, that we provide the communications channels for too much “junk” in the entertainment area. In addition, more and more nonengineers are making important engineering decisions. In the personal arena, the salary advantage that engineers once enjoyed is rapidly eroding.
“It is conceded by leading practical electricians that it would be entirely practicable now to light the city of Buffalo (distance 20 miles) with power furnished by Niagara Falls.”

articleTitle: Computer science and engineering: Laying claim to a new discipline: If engineering is to lay claim to the new computer field, it needs to widen its perspective and regard the computer as more than a tool
abstract: The early mathematical aspects of what is today called computer science originated from the use of computers as sophisticated desk calculators to solve numerical problems [photo], first using scaling of integers in “fixed point” notation and later automatically handling the decimal point through routines or hardware. In those days, the primary role of the electrical engineer was to design a machine that could carry out these computations with the greatest affordable speed, reliability, and cost-effectiveness. Shortly after, the same logical processes for symbol manipulation that enabled computers to do fast arithmetic were used to great advantage for handling, sorting, and processing alphanumeric information in the business world. This activity evolved into what has come to be known as data processing.

articleTitle: View from the top: Planning a successful enterprise: Most business failures are not due to product or service shortfall, but to lack of planning and financial and marketing savvy
abstract: If you are thinking of starting your own company, then the following comments about my experience may help you avoid some common mistakes. I must admit that I did not start my venture with the type of preparation that would ensure a high probability of success.

articleTitle: The hills are alive … with the synthesis of music: Digital synthesizers are outpacing their older analog counterparts, particularly in the area of commercial music
abstract: Computers — you can't seem to get away from them these days. They are found in homes, schools, factories, cars — and now, even in music. Michael Jackson's top song “Beat It,” the soundtrack for the hit movie Flashdance, and even last year's Super Bowl all used a special kind of computer known as a digital synthesizer. The next time you hear “Beat It,” or the title song from Flashdance, listen to the introductory music — what you hear is the Synclavier II, probably the most popular digital synthesizer today. The Synclavier (made by the New England Digital Corp., White River Junction, Vt.) was also used in the soundtracks for the movies Chariots of Fire and Blue Thunder, in the television program “The Powers of Matthew Starr,” in NBC-TV station breaks, and in Genesis's album “Abacab.”

articleTitle: The rise of the writing class: The need for written communication skills has given rise to an effort to give EEs better training as students or to send them back to school on the job
abstract: Rick Thornberg is a young engineering graduate recently hired by an electronics firm in Richmond, Va. His first job evaluation was positive in every area but communication skills, in which his supervisor rated him poor and recommended an in-plant writing course. “I'm not surprised,” Rick says. “I avoided writing all my life and now, ironically, I spend a good third of my work week, and a part of every weekend, composing reports. Each one takes me a long time because I barely know the basics of composition. When I'm done, the writing is still dreadful.”

articleTitle: How leaders become managers: Natural leaders, with training, evolve into professional managers. This transition is the greatest challenge to career development
abstract: Two issues about management are making the rounds these days, and generating a great deal of heat — if not much light. The first has to do with the difference between leaders and managers and the question “Is a leader a manager and, conversely, are managers leaders?” The second issue calls up the current debate between rationality and intuition, which was brought to focus by Thomas Peters and Robert Waterman in their best-selling book In Search of Excellence. Messrs. Peters and Waterman say that it is high time that we move away from our preoccupation with rational management and toward an “esthetic, intuitive” type of management. Since the two issues are interrelated, in responding to one, we shall be dealing with both.

articleTitle: EE at work: Communication — It's not just talk: Getting the word around — Quickly and accurately — Had led to a burgeoning field for EEs who can design systems that are fast and flexible
abstract: Worldwide communication today takes many forms. Among them are teleconferencing, data transmission, and microwave, not to mention everybody's old standby, the telephone. Another basic form of communication is via the printed word, and this, too, has undergone a revolution [see box].

articleTitle: Local area networks: Local area networks — An interconnection of computers and peripherals in adjacent rooms or buildings — Can provide cost-effective communications
abstract: The proliferation of computers of all sizes — from personal computers to business computer systems — has created a need for these systems to interact effectively with one another despite their very different technical specifications. Within short distances (10 kilometers or less), local area networks — systems of computers and peripherals connected together in adjacent rooms and buildings — are the current trend [Fig. 1]. The ultimate goal of these systems is for any computer or intelligent device, such as a video display terminal, printer, phone, text editor, facsimile machine, or telex, to communicate with a similar device on the network or to share resources. Uses to which LANs are put include word processing, file accessing and transfer, teleconferencing, electronic mail, and so on. Communication occurs within the network or with other local networks by means of gateways.

articleTitle: The great oral examination face-off! Psychological warfare at its best: The examiner's goal is to rattle the student, while the victim coolly counterattacks. Both should wear dark glasses
abstract: From the standpoint of each individual examiner, the basic purposes of the oral examination are few and simple: to make the examiner appear smarter and trickier than either the examinee or the other examiners, thereby preserving his or her self-esteem, and to crush the examinee, thereby avoiding the messy and time-wasting problem of postexamination judgment and decision.
“The Nazi juggernaut was created by engineering, and it is only by engineering that it can be destroyed.”

“Should not the Institute develop men as well as ideas? … give them insight into the problems and practices of the profession, without waiting for a sudden plunge from theory to practice upon graduation?”

articleTitle: EE at work: For a bioengineer, the checkered path to administration: He started out with a biology degree. Several years of training and experience later, this bioengineer helps set policy for the Veterans Administration
abstract: In the early seventies when Steven Wexler was an undergraduate student majoring in biology at the State University of New York at Binghamton, all he knew about his career goals was that he was “interested in health-related fields.” Today, several years and a checkered career path later, he is the assistant chief of bioengineering for the entire Veterans Administration system.

articleTitle: Clinical engineering: An education with a future: The degree to which clinical engineering will be successful depends on the type of educational program its future practitioners select
abstract: In a short time technology has affected every facet of society. This is particularly true in medicine and the delivery of health care services, where solutions to many problems confronting health care professionals involve application of the fundamental aspects of device and systems analysis and design, which are the domain of the engineer.

articleTitle: Ham radio operation: A not-so-amateur pastime: From computer applications to space technology, amateur radio presents a unique opportunity for technical innovation and experimentation
abstract: There is a group of people around the world whose spare time is spent behind metallic boxes laden with audio and frequency controls. These are not people listening to Bruce Springsteen or The Cars on their Yamaha or Marantz stereos. Rather they are amateur radio enthusiasts, or ham operators, as they are frequently called.

articleTitle: The art of effective persuasion: Understanding other people's behavioral patterns can often help you communicate and persuade more effectively
abstract: A ceramic engineer brought to his supervisor's attention a type of glass he had created that turned dark when exposed to sunlight and turned clear again when brought into a normally lighted room. His boss, the firm's research and development chief, remarked, “Golly, Bob, I think you've got something there. You should let marketing take a look at it.”

articleTitle: A bright future for fiber optic communications: New developments in fiber optic technology are transforming lightwave communications into one of the fastest growing areas of electronics
abstract: Imagine ocean water so transparent that you could see clearly the deepest depths of the sea. Such is the incredible clarity of some kinds of glass developed over the past decade, which have transformed lightwave communications into one of the fastest growing areas of electronics.

articleTitle: Transforming the image of the engineer: The challenge to engineers is to change their image by making their presence felt in in civic, governmental, and professional affairs
abstract: The engineering profession is one of the finest professions today. It attracts the brightest students, as evidenced by scores on ACT and other achievement tests. Engineering education is sharply aimed at improving problem-solving skills as opposed to learning by rote. The engineering education environment is also among the most intense of any professional education program. Unfortunately, many engineers do not realize this, and the general public is unaware of the importance of engineering to society. It is the responsibility of upcoming engineers to change the image of the engineering profession — the way in which engineers are perceived by the public and the way in which they see themselves.

articleTitle: Jobs across the sea: Working abroad offers professional, personal, and financial rewards but demands maximum flexibility and several years' experience on home turf
abstract: Does the idea of working abroad appeal to your sense of adventure? If so, you'll be happy to know that representatives from international engineering firms agree that the experience of working in a foreign country provides professional, personal, and financial rewards as well.

articleTitle: EE at work: The precise science of instrumentation: The EE who goes into instrumentation design must be prepared to deal with very demanding requirements and be a perfectionist at heart
abstract: High tech demands exquisite precision. When time is measured in nanoseconds and tolerances in parts per million, it is imperative that the instruments used be as exact as the state of the art can make them. For want of an off pulse in a gate, a whole system may crash; for want of 0.5 millivolt, a wrong diagnosis in a serious illness may be made.

articleTitle: Are SPACs effective? SPACs can be effective in increasing professional awareness and interest in branch activities, but branch officers have to maintain the momentum
abstract: The IEEE's goals in supporting Student Professional Awareness Conferences is to help the academic community address the ethical, social, and economic issues that affect the profession of engineering, thereby increasing professional awareness among electrical engineering students. Student Branches that sponsor SPACs have secondary, but also important, goals: to increase membership and participation in Branch activities and to improve campuswide awareness of the IEEE. To what extent is the SPAC program succeeding? After evaluating three SPACs held in the fall of 1983 at Vanderbilt University, Nashville; Tennessee Technological University, Cookeville; and the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, we have concluded that SPACs can be very effective in meeting some of these goals, but only if a Branch is already dynamic and well organized.

articleTitle: Engineer or technologist: A matter of degree? Part III: The quality of EET programs varies widely. Adherence to uniform standards will help to clarify career options and opportunities
abstract: The electrical engineering profession has come of age in a relatively short time. Just 20 years ago, work options available in electrical engineering were limited to people with bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees in power, electronics, and communications.

articleTitle: Surviving the firing line: As the shakeout in the computer industry intensifies, many EEs are unexpectedly losing their jobs. Be prepared, in case you're caught in the line of fire
abstract: There are many ways to be fired, and just as many reasons. An employer may tell you that “it isn't working out,” that “you are being given a chance to resign,” or that “you are being given notice.” On the gentler side, you may be told that the company needs to reduce the workforce and that “you're on the list,” or that “you have been selected as one of those to be released.”

articleTitle: View from the top: The race for high-tech supremacy: In order to maintain market superiority, high-tech industries must increase R&D efforts; government, academia, and industry need to join forces
abstract: High-tech industries will be the basic industries of tomorrow and, therefore, the cornerstone of the economy of any country that wants to be in a leadership position. In the United States, the strengths of the industry are innovation, a competitive free-market environment, skilled labor, and a broad and technically educated infrastructure. But the U.S. high-tech industry also has problems — mainly the cost and availability of capital, a diffuse research and development effort, and inattention to manufacturing technology and quality. In order for the United States to keep its competitive edge — particularly against its major trading partners, such as Japan — R&D efforts need to be stepped up, and a new relationship must be forged among government, academia, and industry.

articleTitle: On the job with three co-ops: Co-op programs give students a chance to try out the “real thing” before graduation. The experience sometimes leads to surprising discoveries
abstract: Co-op work gives students a chance to investigate their chosen careers before graduation, and the experience is sometimes very revealing. One co-op student, for example, discovered that his real interests lay in a different area of electrical engineering than he had originally intended. To another student, the co-op experience highlighted the reality gap between the classroom and actual on-site work. Still another discovered that she really liked what she was doing. The overriding common denominator of these students' experiences, however, was the feeling they got that they were being treated like “real engineers.”

articleTitle: A look at computer networks through a system of layers: The design of computer networks is explained through an example that employs the ISO/ANSI reference model
abstract: Some of this work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy by the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under Contract No. W-7405-Eng-48.

articleTitle: EE at work: On the fast track with the Navy: The government worker's image may be a little tarnished, but working for the Navy has given this EE unmatched responsibility and advancement
abstract: Some people think of government workers as some low form of life,” says Brian Wynne, an electronics engineer with the Naval Air Development Center (NADC) in Warminster, Pa. “They have this image of us as drones who do nothing but sit around and shuffle papers all day. However, I'm very satisfied with my work,” he continues. “There are many good jobs like mine in government that offer satisfying work and responsibility and give you excellent experience.”

articleTitle: View from the top: At Intel, decision-making without walls: Effective decision-making, says the president of Intel, means striking a balance between the forces of knowledge and the power of experience
abstract: A major transition is under way in industry and commerce across the United States. We hear about it in such terms as “sunrise versus sunset” or “high-tech versus smokestack” industries. At the same time, we hear politicians constantly talk about changes in industrial policy. Underneath all these seemingly dynamic clichés, a major shift in the nature of work itself is taking place. Word processors are replacing typewriters, computer-controlled machinery is replacing manual work, and maintenance engineers are replacing production workers. It is clear from all this movement that as work changes, the worker — the person who makes it all happen — must change also.

articleTitle: New horizons for communications satellites: New technology is directed at alleviating interference and congestion by using higher frequencies and achieving greater capacity per orbital slot
abstract: Back in 1945, British science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke envisioned the tremendous possibilities of having a stationary communications relay station in the sky. In an article that was largely ignored, Clarke proposed the revolutionary use of rockets to launch satellites into orbit some 22 235 miles above the earth's surface. At this altitude a satellite appears motionless relative to the earth and is known as a geosynchronous satellite.

articleTitle: From Maxwell to Marconi: The genesis and birth of radio: A 30-year span saw the evolution of radio communications from an experimental novelty to an international commodity
abstract: Radio communications had its genesis in the equations of James Clerk Maxwell (1831–79). Maxwell, a Scottish physicist and teacher, first gained recognition for his research on color vision and later did important work on the kinetic theory of gases [Fig. 1]. Maxwell was also interested in the relationship between electricity and magnetism, and in 1861, while a physics professor at King's College in London, he published a paper entitled “On Physical Lines of Force,” in which he presented a mechanical model of the electric and magnetic fields. At that time scientists still believed that all space was filled with an invisible fluid medium called ether. Maxwell's model represented the electric and magnetic fields as whirling vortices that interacted with each other in the ether.

articleTitle: The IEEE McNaughton learning resource centers: One student branch's initiative provided the impetus for the chain of McNaughton Learning Centers that have sprung up around Canada
abstract: In the academic year 1977–78, the University of Manitoba in Winnipeg, Canada, offered its IEEE Student Branch the use of a large vacant laboratory on the top floor of the engineering building. With the support of their Regional Director, G. F. Glass, the Branch persuaded the IEEE Winnipeg Section to advance them funds to clean up and paint the place. Later, the Section provided more money, which was used for work benches and to establish a facility for satellite tracking, microprocessor study, and personal ham radio projects.

I received a letter from a concerned Branch Chairman recently. He described his Chapter as large, numbering 500–600 members, but expressed his discouragement over the lack of participation in Branch activities in spite of such high numbers. He went on to describe some activities the Branch had scheduled; they sounded interesting and enjoyable, yet student response was poor. I sympathize with this Chairman. His is a problem that is also plaguing other Branches.

This opening structure is the Bell System's display in Epcot's Future World, which is designed to spiral the adventurer through the dramatic history of human communications.

articleTitle: New roles for EEs as volunteers
abstract: For many, volunteering is a nice way of giving while refining technical skills and acquiring some new ones.

articleTitle: 10 Centennial students make IEEE history: They came from all Regions of the IEEE; they mingled with the giants of the past and the greats of the present, and they left feeling a little taller themselves
abstract: Ten Outstanding Centennial Students recently spent four active days attending meetings, receptions, luncheons, and banquets as they rubbed elbows with 20th-century electrical engineering greats such as Ian M. Ross, president of AT&T Bell Labs, and John Bardeen, two-time Nobel Prize winner in physics and co-inventor of the transistor. All their travel, lodging, and meal expenses were picked up by the IEEE. The special event? The IEEE Centennial Celebration in Boston, Mass., May 12 through May 15.

articleTitle: MIT students meet PAC-THING: The lesson in this annual engineering contest is not in if you win or lose, but in how well you design
abstract: Early in the morning of November 21, 1983, a standing-room-only crowd jammed the largest lecture hall of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. They cheered wildly as 180 students battled head to head in a 4 foot by 8 foot sandpit until a single victor emerged. This was not a takeoff on Dungeons and Dragons or even a remote cousin to mud wrestling. These combatants were engineering students earning course credits in an engineering design course by taking part in a yearly back-to-basics engineering contest initiated by Professor Woodie Flowers, course coordinator.

It takes a lot of work to write an editorial that is thematic, coherent, and interesting. I usually begin with some brainstorming about a month before the deadline and organize my basic ideas. Then procrastination sets in. I usually claim to work best under pressure, but in reality I wish I could get my act together long enough to get the article written and typed a week in advance to compensate for inevitable unscheduled delays.
News from various IEEE student branches around the world.

articleTitle: View from the top: Communications: Some futurethink about a leading technology: The author predicts greater communications capability, with fibers leading the way, and hopes we will continue to escape the Orwellian prediction
abstract: The IEEE Centennial year of 1984 seems an appropriate time to talk about the future of communications. George Orwell's famous novel 1984 has given an inescapable aura to this year — a year in which the absolute control of information dissemination is made possible by the invention of the two-way video system known as the telescreen. In the 35 years since the publication of Orwell's book, the technology for systems like Big Brother's telescreen has been developed. Economics and the needs of society, however, have steered the evolution of communications capability in other directions. Fortunately, much of the world has escaped the Orwellian prediction.

Whenever I begin to think of the year 1984, I am reminded of George Orwell's novel 1984, which gives a futuristic view of life in that year, as the author envisioned it when writing the novel in 1948. Using hindsight; it is extremely interesting to analyze which of his predictions became reality and to compare how they evolved figuratively within the literature and historically within our society.

More than 18 percent of the quarter million members of the IEEE are Student Members. Last year, student membership grew more than 12 percent, twice the 6 percent overall growth of IEEE membership. Student Members are, in large part, the future Members, Senior Members, and Fellows of the Institute. This is a healthy accelerated trend for the profession because of the contribution the IEEE can make to student performance and career preparation.

articleTitle: Time-tested methods for effective time management: Regardless of what you think time is, these techniques will make your personal and professional life more productive
abstract: What is time? For most, it is something elusive of which there is never enough. Other people think it is something that flies. And yet others think it is money!

articleTitle: Dr. Coleman is number one Branch Counselor: A lot of talent and hard work go into guiding student activities. UNCC's Dr. Coleman obviously has the right stuff
abstract: What is it about Robert J. Coleman that has propelled him into the first rank of IEEE Student Branch counselors? Talent is certainly part of it. The 43-year-old electrical engineer, who is an associate professor on the faculty of the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, has successfully balanced a full teaching load with a heavily weighted schedule of student-oriented activities, in addition to his occasional consulting assignments.

Why do we have student activities in the IEEE? It is because the IEEE leadership recognizes where the future practitioners of the electrical engineering profession, and the future strength of the Institute, will come from. The well-being of the electrical engineering community and the quality of its contribution to society depend on the preparation of the graduates entering the field. The IEEE contributes to that preparation through student activities.

articleTitle: Across the Atlantic: Networks of friendship: Region 8 has been immensely successful in building networks of friendship that transcend national, cultural, religious, and educational boundaries
abstract: Unlike the homogeneous personality that is prevalent among IEEE Regions in the United States, Region 8, which encompasses Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, is marked by differences in language, culture, religion, and education. Thus, initiating and then maintaining a high level of interest in IEEE student activities has always been a challenge requiring considerable time and energy. Our task has been further burdened by the challenge from national engineering societies that already represent the electrical engineering profession, and student organizations that already exist within the various engineering schools. Nevertheless, our efforts have paid off, and Region 8 has grown from one Branch in 1961 to 42 in 1984 and from a student membership of 200 in 1965 to more than 2000 presently.

articleTitle: C. Richard Johnson Jr.: An outstanding young EE: Do electrical engineering, academia, and international interests make a winning combo? Ask the winner of two coveted Eta Kappa Nu awards
abstract: If one word could describe C. Richard Johnson Jr., a professor of electrical engineering at Cornell University, New York, and the 1983 recipient of the C. Holmes MacDonald Outstanding Teacher Award for young electrical engineering professors, it would have to be diversified — in talent, interests, and experience. Using opportunities in your environment to become diversified, well-rounded individuals is advice that the 34-year-old professor also stresses to students. “Students should strive for closer contact with faculty and take advantage of their expertise,” says Dr. Johnson. “They should also seek to benefit from the enriching aspects of the university itself. I realize that an electrical engineering curriculum is demanding, but opportunities such as these should not be taken for granted.”

articleTitle: Reading up books: Bioengineering: A beginner's bibliography: A good bioengineer must have a solid background in engineering principles and then in biological applications. Here are some books to get you started
abstract: Bioengineering is different things to different people. To a nurse with a broken power cord on a blood pressure monitor, bioengineering is what gets it fixed. To a medical researcher, bioengineering is the design of instrumentation to measure something. To your grandfather with a heart pacemaker, bioengineering is what keeps him going. Using a textbook definition, bioengineering is the application of physical and mathematical principles to biological and medical problems. That covers a lot of ground. Bioengineering can be the use of metallurgy to develop replacement hip joints, or the use of plastics to replace blood vessels, or the signal processing of ultrasonic echo.

articleTitle: Reading up books: A review of circuit analysis texts: Text selection for circuit analysis classes can be difficult. The emergence of texts that can be used by students as learning aids may provide one answer
abstract: Every electrical engineering curriculum has at least one course at the sophomore or junior level titled Circuit Analysis or Systems Analysis, with the systems course also usually oriented toward circuits. Such a course sequence is a staple of all EE curricula for very good reasons. In the first place, these courses offer an early opportunity to reinforce mathematical tools by application. They also offer an opportunity to build on electrical concepts learned in physics. Many important courses that come later build on the abilities developed in these courses. The knowledge gained from these courses also forms the foundation for several branches of electrical engineering.

articleTitle: A controller-recorder for the Get Away Special: This award-winning student paper describes a microprocessor-based controller that will monitor experiments in the space shuttle's GAS container
abstract: The Get Away Special program, which was started by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration in 1976 [see page 33], offers unique opportunities for researchers to perform experiments in space. However, no control is available from space shuttle personnel to operate the experiments once they are inside the GAS canister. One way of building a certain amount of control into the canister is through a Payload Actuation and Control System, a microprocessor-based controller with an integral data recorder [Fig. 1]. Such a system was developed by me and integrated into the first GAS payload, which flew on the STS-4 on June 28, 1982. Approximate cost of electronic components and materials to build a single PACS is $1000.

articleTitle: Reading up books: Readings in communications: A historical review: A good approach for a student interested in communications is to trace its historical development through the literature of the times
abstract: Few disciplines in the field of electrical engineering can claim to be as prolific or to have as much impact on our society as the field of communications. In fewer than 150 years, this technology has taken us from the simple wonders of the telephone and telegraph to the truly spectacular advances in space technology. With the aid of computers of the highest performance levels, satellites today can survey activities on the ground from space with a resolution of approximately 1 meter. With just as much ease, they can beam information from continent to continent and gather, process, and disseminate important meteorological and scientific data.

articleTitle: 1984 Outstanding branch counselors/advisors: This award recognizes those counselors and advisors who truly motivate their students to higher levels of technical and professional competence
abstract: Our thanks and congratulations to these 10 individuals who provide their Branches and Branch Chapter members with the encouragement and guidance necessary to develop their leadership and organizational abilities. They also demonstrate true professionalism by their actions, not just their words. Each of them has been awarded an Outstanding Branch Counselor/Advisor certificate and a $500 check donated jointly by the Regional Activities and Technical Activities Boards of the IEEE.

articleTitle: Reading up books: Computer-aided circuit analysis and design: A discussion of the role of the digital computer in circuit analysis and design is followed by a review of current literature
abstract: The impact of the digital computer in circuit analysis and design has changed the electrical engineer's outlook: EEs are now able to analyze circuits they could not have hoped to solve analytically 20 years ago.
